planting.note: Root cuttings in spring when warmth speeds callusing.

directions: Named for the way its narrow, slightly succulent leaves ring the stem in distinct whorls rather than opposite pairs, this species has one of the widest natural ranges of any hoya, spanning from India through southern China and across Southeast Asia to Indonesia and the Philippines. Train the thin, wiry stems onto a small trellis or let them trail from a hanging basket, and grow in bright filtered light with a chunky, fast-draining mix that dries out between waterings. Clusters of waxy cream flowers with a deep maroon, wine-colored throat give rise to the common name claret hoya, and they carry a light evening fragrance. Established plants tolerate brief dry spells well thanks to their water-storing foliage, but resent being left in cold, wet mix.

As the name suggests, this Southeast Asian climber carries notably wide, oval leaves compared to many narrow-leaved trade hoyas, with a thick, leathery texture that stores water well. It ranges naturally across Borneo, Java, peninsular Malaysia, Myanmar, Sumatra, and Thailand, and the Bornean 'Sarawak Cream' collector form is prized for its pale, creamy flower clusters and heavier leaf substance. Give it a coarse, aroid-style mix, bright indirect light, and a pole or trellis to climb, letting the mix dry fully between waterings since root rot is the main risk. Hoya macrophylla, a name that circulates in the houseplant trade for similarly broad-leaved plants, is treated by some taxonomists as a synonym of this species rather than a fully distinct one.

Collected from the Torricelli mountain range of Papua New Guinea, this epiphytic climber has notably small leaves and correspondingly tiny flowers, true to its name. The pale blooms open in small clusters with a blushed rosy corona at the center, a detail best appreciated with a hand lens given their diminutive size. Mount it on a small slab or grow in a shallow pot of chunky, well-aerated mix, keeping humidity moderate to high and letting the roots dry slightly between waterings. Its understated scale makes it a good fit for a crowded shelf of miniature hoya species rather than a showy centerpiece plant.

common_name: Hairy-Leaf Thread Hoya (New Guinea Fuzzy-Leaf Vine)
directions: This Papua New Guinean species, first described by Rudolf Schlechter in the early 1910s, grows on thin, almost thread-like twining shoots, a delicate habit that benefits from a small moss pole or a few horizontal wires to climb rather than a bulky trellis. Small flowers cluster along the stems once the vine is well rooted, appreciated more for their delicate detail than for size. Keep it in bright, filtered light with high humidity and a chunky mix that drains quickly, since the slender stems have little reserve to recover from prolonged soggy roots.

First described in 1915, this species' name literally means large-flowered, and it is primarily known from Fiji with scattered occurrences in Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and nearby Melanesia. Grow it as a climbing or loosely trailing vine on a support in bright, filtered light, using a coarse, fast-draining mix typical of epiphytic hoya culture. Allow the mix to dry between waterings and maintain warm, humid conditions year-round, since this is a true lowland tropical species with little cold tolerance. It is one of several hoya species native to the Fiji islands alongside the better-known Hoya vitiensis.
